## Live labelling
### Positive, negative, or neutral?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
- You are the annotators. Three product reviews, one vote each: [positive]{.alert}, [negative]{.alert}, or [neutral]{.alert}
- No discussion, no changing your mind. Hands up when I say the label

:::{.fragment}
> "The food was fine, I guess. Service was quick."
:::

:::{.fragment}
> "Took three weeks to arrive, but honestly the best headphones I have owned."
:::

:::{.fragment}
> "I have had worse."
:::

:::{.fragment}
- Did everyone agree? Keep the split in mind. We will come back to it when we measure [annotator agreement]{.alert}
:::
:::

# Why data quality matters 📊 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Garbage in, garbage out
### Why your model can't outrun bad data

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- AI models are only as good as [the data they're trained on]{.alert}
- A better algorithm cannot fix bad data
- Common data problems:
  - Missing important information (e.g., age, income, etc.)
  - Conflicting labels or formats (e.g., "yes" vs "1")
  - Biases, not representative of reality (e.g., gender, race, etc.)
- **Data-centric AI**: Andrew Ng (2021) argues you should [improve the data]{.alert} before you improve the model
  - Check: <https://datacentricai.org/>
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Garbage In, Garbage Out](figures/garbage-in-out.png){width="70%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/garbage-in-out.png"}

Source: [xkcd](https://xkcd.com/1838/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Real-world impact of data quality
### When bad data causes harm

:::{style="margin-top: 60px; font-size: 30px;"}

| Case | What went wrong | Impact |
|------|-----------------|--------|
| Credit scoring | [Data reflected historical gender-based income gaps](https://www.bbc.com/news/business-50365609) | [Lower credit limits]{.alert} for women with similar profiles |
| Facial recognition | [Training data mostly light-skinned faces](http://gendershades.org/) | [Error rates 43x higher]{.alert} for dark-skinned women |
| Criminal risk assessment | [Historical arrest data reflected biased policing](https://www.propublica.org/article/machine-bias-risk-assessments-in-criminal-sentencing) | [Perpetuated racial disparities]{.alert} in sentencing |
| Hiring AI | [Trained on historical (male-dominated) hiring decisions](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-amazon-com-jobs-automation-insight-idUSKCN1MK08G) | [Penalised female candidates]{.alert} |

:::{.fragment}
> In all four cases the model learned [exactly what the data taught it]{.alert}
:::
:::

# Types of machine learning tasks 🎯 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Classification and regression tasks
### The two main types of AI tasks

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
[Classification: Predicting categories]{.alert}

- **Goal**: Assign inputs to discrete categories
- Examples: Email → Spam/Not Spam; Image → Cat/Dog/Bird; Text → Positive/Negative/Neutral
- **Binary classification**: Two classes
- **Multi-class**: Many classes (one per input)
- **Multi-label**: Multiple labels per input
- [How do you define the classes?]{.alert}

:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Classification](figures/classification.png){width="80%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/classification.png"}
:::
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
[Regression: Predicting continuous values]{.alert}

- **Goal**: Predict a continuous numerical value
- Examples: Features → House price; Patient data → Hospital stay length; Weather data → Temperature
- The choice of target variable is [a design decision]{.alert}
- Different targets can lead to very different models

:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Regression](figures/regression.png){width="80%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/regression.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Other common AI tasks
### Beyond classification and regression

:::{style="margin-top: 60px; font-size:30px;"}

| Task | Description | Example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| [Object Detection]{.alert} | Find and locate objects in images | Self-driving cars detecting pedestrians |
| [Segmentation]{.alert} | Label every pixel in an image | Medical imaging (tumour boundaries) |
| [Sequence Labelling]{.alert} | Label each element in a sequence | Named entity recognition in text |
| [Generation]{.alert} | Create new content | ChatGPT, DALL-E, music generation |
| [Ranking]{.alert} | Order items by relevance | Search results, recommendations |

:::{.fragment}
> Each task requires [different types of labels]{.alert} in your dataset!
:::
:::

## Defining your classes
### Classification pitfalls

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Classes should be:
  - **Mutually exclusive**: No overlap between categories
  - **Collectively exhaustive**: Cover all possible cases
  - **Consistently definable**: Clear boundaries
- Common problems:
  - [Ambiguous categories]{.alert}: What counts as "spam"?
  - [Subjective judgments]{.alert}: Is this review "positive"?
  - [Cultural differences]{.alert}: What's "offensive" varies
  - [Evolving definitions]{.alert}: Categories change over time
- Solution: [Clear annotation guidelines]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![A duck or a rabbit?](figures/duck-rabbit.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/duck-rabbit.png"}

Source: [The Independent](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/science/duck-and-rabbit-illusion-b1821663.html)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The proxy problem
### When labels don't measure what you care about

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Often we can't directly measure what we want to predict
- So we use [proxy variables]{.alert} instead, and proxies can mislead
- **Example 01: Predicting "health needs"**
  - What we want: How sick is this patient?
  - Available data: Healthcare spending
  - [Spending ≠ health needs]{.alert}: Black patients had less spent on them due to systemic barriers
  - Algorithm learned: "Black patients need less care" → [Wrong!]{.alert}
- **Example 02: Predicting expertise on social media**
  - What we want: Who is an expert in a field?
  - Available data: Number of followers
  - [Followers ≠ Expertise]{.alert}: Popularity can be gamed or unrelated to domain knowledge
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Model-centric vs. Data-centric AI](figures/data-centric.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/data-centric.png"}

Source: [Andrej Karpathy](https://vimeo.com/274274744)
:::

<br>

- Always ask: [Does this label actually measure what I care about?]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

# Sourcing and collecting data 📥 {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Where do the data come from?
### Common data sources

:::{style="margin-top: 60px; font-size: 28px;"}

| Source | Examples | Considerations |
|--------|----------|----------------|
| [Existing databases]{.alert} | Hospital records, transaction logs | May have missing fields, inconsistent formats |
| [Public datasets]{.alert} | ImageNet, Wikipedia, Common Crawl | May not match your specific domain |
| [Web scraping]{.alert} | Social media, news articles | Legal and ethical concerns |
| [Surveys/Forms]{.alert} | User feedback, questionnaires | Response bias, sampling issues |
| [Sensors/IoT]{.alert} | Cameras, wearables, satellites | Privacy concerns, data volume |
| [Synthetic data]{.alert} | Generated by other models | May not capture real-world complexity |

:::

## How much data do you need?
### The million-dollar question

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [There's no universal answer...]{.alert} it depends on:
  - Task complexity: harder tasks need more data
  - Number of classes/features: more categories = more examples needed
  - Model architecture: deep learning is data-hungry
  - Required accuracy: higher stakes = more data
- [Rule of thumb]{.alert}: Start small, then scale up
- [Scaling laws]{.alert}: Performance improves predictably with more data
  - You can [estimate]{.alert} how much data you'll need by training on subsets and extrapolating
- For most real-world problems, [more high-quality data beats more sophisticated algorithms]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Performance vs. dataset size](figures/scaling-curve.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/scaling-curve.png"}

Source: [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/ai-performance-knowledge-tests-vs-dataset-size)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Selection bias ⚠️ {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## What is selection bias?
### When your data doesn't represent reality

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Selection bias]{.alert}: your training data differ systematically from the cases the model will meet
- Close relatives: sampling bias, distribution shift, survivorship bias
- The model learns patterns that [won't generalise]{.alert}
- [Extremely hard to fix after the fact]{.alert}
- [Prevention is better than cure]{.alert}!
- Always ask: "In what ways might my data not be representative?"
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Selection bias](figures/survivorship-bias.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/survivorship-bias.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survivorship_bias)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Common causes of selection bias
### Where does bias creep in?

:::{style="margin-top: 60px; font-size: 26px;"}

| Type | Description | Example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| [Time bias]{.alert} | Data from the past applied to the future | Training on 2021 data for 2026 predictions |
| [Location bias]{.alert} | Data from one place applied elsewhere | US healthcare model used in India |
| [Demographic bias]{.alert} | Certain groups under/over-represented | Clinical trial with mostly young, white, male participants |
| [Availability bias]{.alert} | Using convenient rather than representative data | Surveying only friends |
| [Response bias]{.alert} | Who responds differs from who doesn't | Online surveys miss offline populations |
| [Long-tail bias]{.alert} | Rare events underrepresented | Self-driving cars: unusual scenarios |

- Try it out: Let's generate an image of a CEO and a nurse using two different models, such as [Qwen](https://qwen.ai/) and [Gemini](https://gemini.google.com). What do you notice?
:::

## Dealing with selection bias
### Mitigation strategies

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Before collection:**

- [List the biases you expect]{.alert} before collecting data
- Design collection to [cover important subgroups]{.alert}
- [Over-sample]{.alert} rare but [important cases]{.alert}

**After collection:**

- Use [data augmentation]{.alert} to increase dataset size
  - Try it out at home! Use an image generator to create variations of the same object (different angles, lighting, etc)
- Use [representative validation sets]{.alert}
- If deploying in new locations: validate on location-specific data
- [Document known limitations]{.alert} of your dataset
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Strategies to reduce bias](figures/bias-mitigation.jpg){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/bias-mitigation.jpg"}

Source: [WisdomPlexus](https://wisdomplexus.com/blogs/ai-bias-in-action-real-world-examples-and-mitigation-strategies/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Labelling data 🏷️ {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Why labelling is hard
### Humans are slow, expensive, and inconsistent

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Most AI models require [labelled data]{.alert}
- Labels come from humans → humans make mistakes
- Common issues:
  - **Inconsistency**: Different people label differently
  - **Ambiguity**: Some examples are genuinely unclear
  - **Mislabelling**: Human errors happen
  - **Fatigue**: Quality drops over time
  - **Expertise**: Some tasks need domain experts
- Labelling is [expensive and time-consuming]{.alert}
  - See [Alexandr Wang's Scale AI](https://scale.com/)
- Quality control is super important!
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Labelling is harder than it looks!](figures/labeling-challenge.jpg){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/labeling-challenge.jpg"}

Source: [Galliot](https://galliot.us/blog/data-labeling-approaches-challenges-tools/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Writing good annotation guidelines
### What annotators actually need from you

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
Good guidelines should include:

1. **Clear definitions**: What does each label mean?
2. **Examples**: Canonical cases for each class
3. **Counter-examples**: What does NOT belong
4. **Edge cases**: How to handle ambiguity
5. **Visual aids**: Screenshots, annotated examples

Best practices:

- [Test guidelines]{.alert} with a small group first
- [Iterate]{.alert} based on confusion and disagreements
- Keep guidelines as [living documents]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![](figures/annotation-guidelines.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/annotation-guidelines.png"}

Source: [Google's Healthcare Text Annotation Guidelines](https://github.com/google/healthcare-text-annotation/blob/master/guidelines/defining-entity-categories.md)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Multiple annotators and agreement {#sec-agreement}
### Reducing individual errors

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 20px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**Why use multiple annotators:**

- Individual annotators make mistakes
- [Multiple annotators → more reliable labels]{.alert}
- Benefits: Catch errors, identify ambiguous cases, assess label quality, reduce biases
- Trade-off: [More expensive]{.alert}

**Aggregation strategies:**

- **Majority vote**: Most common label wins (limitations: ties, equal weighting)
- **Weighted voting**: Trust reliable annotators more
- **Adjudication**: Expert makes final call
- **Keep all labels**: Train on disagreement (for uncertainty research)
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**Measuring agreement (IAA):**

- [Inter-annotator agreement]{.alert}: Do annotators agree?
- High agreement → Labels are reliable
- Low agreement → Problem with guidelines or task
- Common metric: [Cohen's Kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen%27s_kappa) ([Fleiss' Kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleiss%27_kappa) for more than two annotators)

:::{style="text-align: center;"}
**Cohen's Kappa:**
$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

:::{style="font-size: 17px; text-align: left;"}
- $p_o$ (observed agreement): share of items both annotators labelled the same way
- $p_e$ (expected agreement): share they would agree on by chance, given how often each one uses each label
- [[Worked example]{.button}](#sec-appendix-kappa)
:::

| Kappa | Interpretation |
|-------|----------------|
| < 0.20 | Slight |
| 0.21–0.40 | Fair |
| 0.41–0.60 | Moderate |
| 0.61–0.80 | Substantial |
| 0.81–1.00 | Almost perfect |
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Quality control
### Catching mistakes before they reach your model

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Quality control (QC) examples]{.alert}: Examples where you already know the correct answer
- Slip QC examples into the labelling queue [without telling annotators]{.alert}
- Use them to:
  - Monitor annotator accuracy over time
  - Identify annotators who need retraining
  - Catch low-quality work early
- Flag annotators who fail too many QC checks
- Combine with [regular audits]{.alert} of random samples
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![QC examples catch errors](figures/quality-control.jpeg){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/quality-control.jpeg"}

Source: [SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/guide-to-data-labeling)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Building an annotation pipeline
### From guidelines to final dataset

:::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '17px'}}}%%
flowchart TB
    A[📊 Data Selection] --> B[📝 Guideline Design]
    B --> C[👥 Annotator Training]
    C --> D[🧪 Pilot Labelling]
    D --> E{Quality OK?}
    E -->|No| B
    E -->|Yes| F[🏭 Full Labelling]
    F --> G[✅ QC Checks]
    G --> H[📈 Aggregation]
    H --> I[🎯 Final Dataset]
    style E fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style I fill:#90EE90,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**Key stages:**

1. **Select data** stratified by important subgroups
2. **Design guidelines** with clear definitions and examples
3. **Train annotators** and calibrate their judgments
4. **Pilot** on a small sample, iterate on guidelines
5. **Scale up** with ongoing quality control
6. **Aggregate labels** using appropriate strategies
7. **Document** everything for reproducibility
:::
:::
:::

# Summary {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Main takeaways

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 32px;"}

- [Data quality > Algorithm sophistication]{.alert} for most real-world problems

- [Problem framing]{.alert} determines what data you need and how to label it

- [Selection bias]{.alert} is a major source of error. List the biases before you collect

- [Labelling is hard]{.alert}, so write clear guidelines and check the work

- [Multiple annotators]{.alert} improve reliability, but aggregate intelligently

- [Document everything]{.alert}, so your future self will thank you
:::

# Appendix {background-color="#1B3A6B"}

## Cohen's kappa by hand {#sec-appendix-kappa}
### Two annotators labeling 100 product reviews as "positive" or "negative"

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
|  | B: Positive | B: Negative | Total |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **A: Positive** | 40 | 10 | 50 |
| **A: Negative** | 15 | 35 | 50 |
| **Total** | 55 | 45 | 100 |
:::

<br>

- The diagonal (40 and 35) is where A and B agree
- A says "positive" 50% of the time, B says it 55% of the time
:::

:::{.column width=55%}
1. Observed agreement: $p_o = \frac{40 + 35}{100} = 0.75$
2. Chance both say positive: $0.50 \times 0.55 = 0.275$
3. Chance both say negative: $0.50 \times 0.45 = 0.225$
4. Expected agreement: $p_e = 0.275 + 0.225 = 0.50$
5. Kappa: $\kappa = \frac{0.75 - 0.50}{1 - 0.50} = 0.50$, "moderate"

[[Back to the lecture]{.button}](#sec-agreement)
:::
:::
:::
